name: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
title: CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
ai_text: In AI software this weakness shows up mostly in model serving and agent plumbing, where a single request can eat memory or CPU until the service dies. The CVEs sit in vLLM, MCP servers and SDKs, Triton Inference Server, Open WebUI, Transformers and camel. Attackers reach it through ordinary inputs the product accepts: overlong prompts, oversized audio, video or media URLs, endless bytes from a stdio peer, or a regex in a structured output request. Many need no authentication at all. The result is a crashed or stalled worker, exhausted GPU memory, or a whole instance that stops answering. Examples include vLLM, MKP and Triton Inference Server.
description: The product does not properly control the allocation and maintenance of a limited resource.

mitigations.description: Design throttling mechanisms into the system architecture. The best protection is to limit the amount of resources that an unauthorized user can cause to be expended. A strong authentication and access control model will help prevent such attacks from occurring in the first place. The login application should be protected against DoS attacks as much as possible. Limiting the database access, perhaps by caching result sets, can help minimize the resources expended. To further limit the potential for a DoS attack, consider tracking the rate of requests received from users and blocking requests that exceed a defined rate threshold.

Mitigation of resource exhaustion attacks requires that the target system either: recognizes the attack and denies that user further access for a given amount of time, or uniformly throttles all requests in order to make it more difficult to consume resources more quickly than they can again be freed. The first of these solutions is an issue in itself though, since it may allow attackers to prevent the use of the system by a particular valid user. If the attacker impersonates the valid user, they may be able to prevent the user from accessing the server in question. The second solution is simply difficult to effectively institute -- and even when properly done, it does not provide a full solution. It simply makes the attack require more resources on the part of the attacker.
Ensure that protocols have specific limits of scale placed on them.
Ensure that all failures in resource allocation place the system into a safe posture.

consequences.note: If an attacker can trigger the allocation of the limited resources, but the number or size of the resources is not controlled, then the most common result is denial of service. This would prevent valid users from accessing the product, and it could potentially have an impact on the surrounding environment, i.e., the product may slow down, crash due to unhandled errors, or lock out legitimate users. For example, a memory exhaustion attack against an application could slow down the application as well as its host operating system.
In some cases it may be possible to force the product to fail open in the event of resource exhaustion. The state of the product -- and possibly the security functionality - may then be compromised.
